1) Basal cell carcinoma — Most likely given elderly patient with a nonhealing cheek lesion on sun-exposed site; common and can be missed on a superficial or improperly oriented biopsy. Recommend repeat full-thickness/excisional biopsy or deep shave with clear margins and dermatopathology review with deeper sections.

2) Squamous cell carcinoma (cutaneous) — Second most likely; presents as a nonhealing, scaly/crusted or ulcerated lesion on the face in older adults. Also at risk of being missed if initial biopsy sampling missed the diagnostic area. Recommend repeat excisional biopsy and consider nodal exam/imaging if positive.

3) Actinic keratosis / hypertrophic actinic change (including hypertrophic AK or Bowen disease) — Chronic sun damage lesions can be nonhealing and precancerous; superficial biopsy can be nondiagnostic depending on sampling. Management: repeat biopsy or removal and histology.

4) Cutaneous adnexal or sebaceous carcinoma (including Merkel cell tumor less likely) — Less common, can occur on the face in older adults and sometimes yield nondiagnostic initial samples. Recommend full excision and immunohistochemistry if suspected.

5) Chronic infectious or inflammatory ulcer (atypical mycobacterial, deep fungal, cutaneous leishmaniasis, or chronic bacterial colonization / traumatic ulcer) — Less likely than malignancy but considered when biopsies are nondiagnostic. Recommend tissue culture (bacterial/mycobacterial/fungal) and targeted histochemical stains if repeat biopsy still nondiagnostic.

Immediate next actions to confirm diagnosis: repeat, preferably excisional, biopsy of the lesion with oriented deep sections and dermatopathology review (including immunostains as indicated), and send tissue for bacterial/mycobacterial/fungal cultures if clinical suspicion for infection. Conduct focused skin exam and palpate regional lymph nodes; obtain photography of the lesion.
